corrected_value.authors: Dalton M, Davidson M, Keating J.
corrected_value.title: The Assessment of Physiotherapy Practice (APP) is a valid measure of professional competence of physiotherapy students: a cross-sectional study with Rasch analysis.

decisions.location: Results (Measurement invariance evidence), lines 260-264; Discussion, lines 274-280; Reference 4, lines 367-368
decisions.quote:
We chose to examine and present the findings of the 1-factor model because it is the original operationalisation of APP for student performance [
3

5
] and commonly implemented among clinical education programs in ANZ. Overall, model-data fit statistics supported scalar invariance for both the 1-factor and 2-factor solutions across time and contextual factors.
decisions.reason:
Prior adjudication and state files at the supplied context paths do not exist (never-adjudicated work). Using a new multi-site archival dataset (8,979 clinical placement assessments from 1,865 physiotherapy students across 19 ANZ universities), the paper explicitly re-tests the factorial validity (confirmatory factor analysis) and longitudinal/contextual measurement invariance of the original 1-factor structural representation of the APP alongside the competing 2-factor representation. Results (lines 258-264, Table 4) present the measurement invariance tests for the 1-factor CFA model and find scalar invariance across time and contextual factors, and Discussion (lines 274-280) and Conclusion (lines 318-319) explicitly conclude that their multi-site replication study supported the psychometric integrity of both the 1-factor [3–5] and 2-factor [7] representations while finding relative superiority for the 2-factor model. Reference 4 (Dalton, Davidson, & Keating, 2011, J Physiother. 2011;57(4):239–46) is the canonical peer-reviewed journal publication reporting the original cross-sectional Rasch dimensionality/validity study establishing the 1-factor APP structure (whereas sibling target_index 0, Reference 3, is the 2009 ALTC institutional grant final report / original protocol for that same development project, and Reference 5 is the 2012 inter-rater reliability study not re-tested here). The only shipped row (input_row_index 831: Reubenson, Ng, & Gucciardi, 2020, 10.1016/j.jphys.2020.03.009) is Reference 7 (blind target_index 2), a different study by different authors that proposed the competing 2-factor model, so report equivalence with shipped row 831 does not apply. No DOI is printed for Reference 4 in the source text or Crossref metadata file, so doi is omitted. Note: Luna's omission_quote failed validation only because it omitted literal newlines inside '[

decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files at the supplied context paths do not exist (never-adjudicated work). In this multi-site archival replication study (N = 1,865 students across 8,979 clinical placements), the authors empirically re-test both the original 1-factor representation and the 2-factor representation (shipped row input_row_index 831, Reubenson, Ng, & Gucciardi, 2020, 10.1016/j.jphys.2020.03.009, Reference 7 / blind target_index 2) of the Assessment of Physiotherapy Practice (APP). However, blind target_index 0 (Reference 3: Dalton, Keating, & Davidson, 2009, Australian Learning and Teaching Council Final report PP6-28) and blind target_index 1 (Reference 4: Dalton, Davidson, & Keating, 2011, Journal of Physiotherapy 57(4):239-46) are duplicate citations of the same original 1-factor APP development and dimensionality work. The Introduction refers to References 3-5 in the singular as 'The original APP development work provided initial validity (e.g., dimensionality, differential item functioning, discriminant) and reliability (e.g., inter-rater) evidence [3–5]' and cites [3, 4] together for the unidimensional design. Methods (lines 194-196) identifies Reference 3 as 'the original protocol [3]', whereas Reference 4 is the peer-reviewed journal publication reporting the primary empirical cross-sectional Rasch dimensionality/validity study (and Discussion lines 300-306 cites [4, 5, 7], omitting [3], when naming the empirical validation evidence whose limitations this study addresses). Under the codebook rule to prefer the published empirical article over a protocol or preliminary/institutional report and the review instructions to retain only one canonical missing pair when two unmatched targets cite the same original work, target_index 1 (Dalton et al., 2011) is retained as the canonical missing original and target_index 0 (Dalton et al., 2009) is excluded as its duplicate. Note: Luna's omission_quote failed mechanical validation because it stripped literal newlines inside the bracketed citation.
